stances.claim: Of the three accountability tracks, criminal charges would take years to mature and risk reversal on appeal -- a recurring weakness of high-profile prosecutions; the operative critique is that 'probable cause' suffices to file but 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' is required to convict.
stances.rhetorical_move: Pessimistic-realist appraisal of the criminal track with a callback to CJ's recurring filing-standard critique.

stances.claim: Disbarment is governed by the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (April 11, 2023) and covers VP Sara's recent acts; proceedings are 'confidential' until judgment, so CJ explicitly refuses to comment further.

Impeachment is 'a very public political and legal exercise'; if the ground is 'betrayal of public trust,' proceedings can be speedy because no judicial interpretation of the term exists -- meaning is best determined by Congress under separation of powers.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal-pathway endorsement leaning into legislative supremacy on undefined grounds.

stances.claim: Judicial intervention in impeachment is properly limited to grave abuse of discretion -- the only case CJ knows of is Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, per J Carpio Morales) which nullified the second impeachment of CJ Davide for violating the constitutional once-per-year ban.
stances.rhetorical_move: Single-precedent illustration of when judicial intervention is appropriate.

stances.claim: Despite the President's public opposition to impeachment, if filings occur, 'Congress must perform its constitutional duty to process the impeachment till it ends in acquittal or conviction or stoppage by the Court' -- and 'rule of law and due process' must be observed regardless of intent or result.
stances.rhetorical_move: Procedural-duty insistence neutralizing the President's political opposition.

notable_anecdotes.description: VP Sara Duterte's contentious quoted statement: 'Don't worry about my security because I have already contracted an individual, and told him/her that if I am killed, you should also kill BBM (President Marcos), (First Lady) Liza Araneta-Marcos and (Speaker) Martin Romualdez. No joke. No joke...' Later VP Sara claimed the remarks were 'maliciously taken out of logical context.'

President's response invoking sworn duty: 'As the head of the executive department, as well as all public servants, I have a sworn duty to uphold the Constitution and the laws. As a democratic country, we need to uphold the rule of law.' Cascade of officials calling for action: Executive Secretary, DOJ, NBI, PNP, AFP, NSC, House Speaker and representatives, Senate President and senators, and many private citizens urged (1) criminal charges (grave threats, sedition, direct assault, anti-terror); (2) disbarment; (3) impeachment.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Documents the full institutional response cascade.

notable_anecdotes.description: Impeachment procedural map per Constitution: verified complaint by House member OR citizen with endorsement → referral to proper committee → one-third vote to affirm or override Articles; one-third filing constitutes Articles directly and triggers Senate trial → Senate sole power to try and decide → two-thirds concurrence for conviction → judgment may include disqualification from public office.

Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, en banc, per J Conchita Carpio Morales): the one case CJ knows where the SC used 'grave abuse of discretion' to intervene in impeachment -- nullifying the proceeding against CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. for the House's violation of the constitutional ban on impeachment 'against the same official more than once within a period of one year.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Single doctrinal precedent illustrating the narrow judicial role.

one_paragraph_summary: Triggered by Vice President Sara Duterte's contentious statement that she had 'contracted an individual' to kill President Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and Speaker Martin Romualdez if she herself were killed ('No joke. No joke') -- later walked back as 'maliciously taken out of logical context' -- CJ Panganiban walks through the three accountability tracks now invoked against her. Malacañang labeled the statement 'an active threat'; the Executive Secretary, DOJ, NBI, PNP, AFP, NSC, House Speaker and representatives, Senate President and senators, and many private citizens urged criminal charges (grave threats, sedition, direct assault, anti-terror law), disbarment, and impeachment. On the criminal track, CJ flags the structural weakness -- sensational cases covered by tri-media and won at the lower courts 'only to be reversed on appeal due to failure to prosecute, or insufficient evidence, or egregious legal errors' -- and renews his recurring critique that 'probable cause' is enough to file but 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' is required to convict: 'why prosecute when there is not enough evidence to convict?' On disbarment, the new Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability of April 11, 2023 covers the VP's acts but proceedings are confidential until judgment, so CJ desists from comment. On impeachment, the column lays out the full constitutional pathway -- exclusive House initiation via verified complaint (by member or citizen with endorsement), committee referral, one-third House vote to affirm Articles (or directly filed by one-third); Senate sole power to try and decide; two-thirds concurrence to convict; possible disqualification from public office. If the ground is 'betrayal of public trust' -- uniquely lacking judicial interpretation -- proceedings can be speedy, and 'in my humble opinion, its meaning can best be determined by Congress' under separation of powers, with judicial intervention reserved for 'grave abuse of discretion,' as in the only example CJ cites: Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, en banc, per J Conchita Carpio Morales), nullifying the second impeachment of CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. for violating the constitutional ban on impeachment 'against the same official more than once within a period of one year.' Despite the President's stated opposition to impeachment, CJ insists Congress 'must perform its constitutional duty to process the impeachment till it ends in acquittal or conviction or stoppage by the Court' -- and that 'regardless of their intent and result, the rule of law and due process are observed.'
